== 1. The source, and the extraction that had been the blocker ==

The British **War Office, *Manual of Cryptography*** — the copy in the project Drive
(`1nQQ0JYItDYDCdPL7PxsmS6XCB1tZwPJS`, 5,883,419 bytes), a rip of the Aegean Park Press facsimile
(ISBN 0-89412-042-5, "Reproduction of a classical, historical document, c. 1914"; the original's
print code, "(B364) 20, 10/14 H&S 1139wo", is on its title page). Round 4 had opened the book only
far enough to capture its contents page and list of works consulted, on the assumption that its
diagrams would not survive extraction. The diagrams don't — the tables are bitmap figures — but the
**rules and the printed cryptograms are plain text**, and that is all a recipe needs.

*Reading method, because it shaped the round:* `read_file_text` on the Drive PDF returns the text
from the start, and past a certain size the harness returns the start and the end of the requested
window with the middle elided; the same call with the same arguments reproduces the same window, so
each pass moved the window by changing `max_chars` (15 000 → 52 000 → 56 000 → 60 000) until
chapter III(a) fell inside it. Recorded for the next book: the fix is to slide the window, not to
re-request it.

*What turned out not to be needed:* archive.org's own scan of this manual, referred to by the
facsimile's credit line as `manualofcryptogrO00Obrit`; its `_djvu.txt` is not served ("the item you
have requested has a problem with one or more of the metadata files"), and the only identifier
matching `manualofcryptogr*` there remains Sacco's unrelated manual. The Wikimedia Commons 1911
scan (108 pages, 12.12 MB, photographed from the Marshall Foundation's copy) was located as an
alternative source, but the Drive copy's text layer made it unnecessary.

== 2. Chapter III(a) §2 — the Zigzag Transposition cipher ==

The rule, as printed (p. 21): *"In this cipher the letters of the text are written out in columns,
each containing a pre-arranged number of spaces. The letters are written up and down alternate
columns, beginning at the top or bottom of a certain column, and the cryptogram is formed by reading
off the lines of letters."* — the starting end ("top or bottom of a certain column") is part of what
the correspondents agree.

The worked example, on p. 22, takes the same sentence §1 had used, "**A reconnaissance made
yesterday across the river found no traces of the enemy**", with **8 letters to a column**,
*"dummy letters being used, if necessary, to complete the table"*, and prints the cryptogram in
five-letter groups:

```
AMAOS NOMYR EDRSD TEFEC ECTNR NUCNY
AHUAE LOAEY EOCEL NSSAR FEHSN STDIR
STTAI ERVEO FO
```

**The convention the vector fixes.** The sentence is 65 letters; 8-letter columns give a 9-column
table, so 72 cells and **7 dummies**, and the book's cryptogram is 72 letters. Reconstructing the
table from the printed cryptogram shows exactly one reading that returns the sentence: column 1 is
written **top to bottom**, column 2 bottom to top, alternating; the dummies are the trail's last
seven cells and read `FULLSTO`. The trail is the sentence followed by `FULLSTO`, and every one of
the 65 message letters lands on its printed letter; the alternatives were checked and rejected
(starting at the bottom, 6/65 matches; an eight-column table, 5/65). The book's own diagram, which
would have shown the arrows, is one of the bitmap figures that did not survive.

**The recipe.** `zigzagTransposition` — *Zigzag Transposition (War Office 1914)*, category
Classical. Arguments: letters per column (default 8), the end the first column starts at, the
padding letters (cycled when shorter than the gap), and the mode. Like the manual, the text is
taken as capitals with non-letters dropped. `tests/war-office-manual-ciphers.test.mjs` pins the
printed cryptogram (and reads it back in the book's five-letter groups), two hand-checkable
12-letter mini cases — `ABCDEFGHIJKL` in 3-letter columns → `AFGLBEHKCDIJ`, and the bottom-start
variant → `CDIJBEHKAFGL` — the padding cycle, and the refusal when a received cryptogram is not a
whole number of columns.

== 3. Chapter III(a) §4 — the Nihilists' Cipher ==

The printed rule (p. 26): *"This cipher, which is said to have been used by Nihilists, is based upon
the principle of double transposition. A keyword is agreed upon by the correspondents, and a number
is obtained from the alphabetical order of the letters forming it. Thus the word 'Thames' would
represent 631425, T being the 6th letter in alphabetical order of the six letters forming the
keyword, H the 3rd letter, and so on."* A square is filled with the message in its natural order;
a second square re-labels both sides with those numbers and the letters keep their coordinates;
the cryptogram is read off the lines. The N.B.: blanks are filled with dummy letters, *"the less
frequently occurring letters of the alphabet being used for this purpose"* — here `QXYZ`.

The example's keyword is **Thames** (side 6, so 36 cells) and the message **"The sixth division
will attack at dawn"** — 32 letters, four dummies — printed as:

```
ZQWXNYIOSNIWXETSHIAALTLT
IDTIHVAACTKD
```

**The transform the vector fixes.** With `P` the keyword's ranks in position order
(`Thames → [6,3,1,4,2,5]`), the cryptogram square is `C[i][j] = orig[P[i]][P[j]]` (1-based): both
sides of the square are re-labelled by the same permutation. Under that rule the message plus
`QXYZ` reproduces the printed 36 letters **byte for byte**, and the inverse reading returns
`THESIXTHDIVISIONWILLATTACKATDAWNQXYZ` — the direction is confirmed rather than assumed, which
matters because the printed coordinate sentence ("the letter W given by the co-ordinates 5 and 3 …
is placed in the column marked 5 in the line marked 3") is ambiguous without the figure.

**One or more tables.** The section closes by noting that *"the tables used must always be
completely filled"* and that a longer message needs *"one or more tables"* — so the recipe fills
successive side×side squares, each with the same permutation, padding only the last. A
hand-checkable case caught the omission when this was first coded: a 13-letter message under a
three-letter keyword silently lost everything past the first nine letters until the chunking was
added. The new test pins the multi-table path (`DEFENDTHEEASTTWENTYTWO` under `ABC` → itself plus
five dummies, decrypt back) as well as the single-table examples.

**The recipe.** `nihilistSquare` — *Nihilists' Square (War Office 1914)*, category Classical:
keyword, padding letters, mode; capitals with non-letters dropped. Refusals: an empty keyword, a
one-letter keyword, a cryptogram that does not fill whole squares, an empty message.

== 4. What the manual still offers ==

The contents page was captured in round 4; with chapter III(a) now legible, the remaining backlog
is specific:

* **§1, the Hebrew Transposition cipher** — the same reconnaissance sentence written in 23-letter
  lines and read another way; the rule text came through but its worked grid is a bitmap, so it is
  a candidate, not yet a vector.
* **§3, the Permutation cipher** — permutations of four figures (the book names 1324, 1243, 3214)
  applied in succession to "Delay departure of transports until you receive further orders from
  headquarters"; a keyed multiple-permutation transposition with no equivalent in the kitchen.
  The next candidate from this source.
* **§5, the Federal Army cipher (A)** — word transposition along a six-column route (up the sixth,
  down the first, up the fifth, down the second, up the fourth, down the third); the manual prints
  the route but no cryptogram.
* **Chapters IV–V** — diagonal transposition, stencil, Federal Army (B), double slide figure,
  Bacon's, the vowel cipher, Napoleon's cipher or *tableau de Porta*, Wheatstone's cryptograph,
  Marmont's figure cipher, the Masonic cipher, Schotti's dot cipher, the line cipher.
